justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 740.5 was anchored closely to the last observed price, with very little assumed drift, as short-term price action tends to mean-revert around recent levels absent a clear catalyst. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 743, reflecting a mild positive bias consistent with a low-volatility trending environment. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 748 continues that gradual upward slope, essentially extrapolating a slow trend while acknowledging that a month is long enough for meaningful directional movement to accumulate.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to realized and implied volatility at each horizon. For the one-day interval, the 35-point range reflects typical daily fluctuation assuming moderate volatility — roughly plus or minus 2–2.5% around the point estimate. As the horizon extends to one week, the interval widens to 66 points, consistent with volatility scaling roughly with the square root of time. By one month, the 127-point range captures the substantially larger uncertainty that accumulates over four to five weeks of potential price movement, macro shifts, and positioning changes.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises — such as an unexpected inflation print or central bank policy shift — that could trigger sharp moves well beyond normal daily ranges. Geopolitical shocks, liquidity events, or a broader risk-off episode in financial markets could also produce outsized moves. On the upside, a strong earnings season or unexpected policy easing could push prices meaningfully above the upper bounds.

It is worth noting that these intervals, while wide by everyday standards, are still probabilistic and not guarantees. A 90% confidence interval by construction leaves a 10% probability of outcomes outside the stated range. In practice, financial price distributions tend to have fat tails, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. This means the true probability of breaching these bounds may be modestly higher than 10%, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail risks have more time to materialize.
